newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: U.N. war crimes body prepares to try Croat General.
newsitem.headline: U.N. war crimes body prepares to try Croat General.

text.p: The United Nations' war crimes tribunal on Tuesday begins the trial of its highest-ranking war crimes suspect to date, Croat General Tihomir Blaskic.

Blaskic, 36, is charged with crimes against humanity committed against Moslems in the Lasva Valley area of central Bosnia during 1992 and 1993 when he was a colonel commanding Bosnian Croat (HVO) forces in the area.
He voluntarily surrendered to the tribunal in April 1996 and has been held under house arrest at a secret Hague location since then.
The Blaskic case has created tension between the tribunal and Croatia, which has stood behind him.

He was promoted to a senior post in Croatia's regular army after his indictment for war crimes and decorated by Croatian President Franjo Tudjman for his war service, drawing criticism from the United States.

The trial date has been put back several times as the tribunal has struggled to get access to evidence for both the prosecution and defence, going as far as to try to subpoena the defence ministers of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia.

Bosnian Moslems and Croats in the Lasva Valley fought side-by-side against separatist Serb forces when civil war first broke out in Yugoslavia in 1992, but the alliance collapsed in 1993 as they turned their guns on each other in a bitter territorial struggle.
Both sides swapped accusations of gruesome massacres as villages were torched and people driven from their homes.
The tribunal says Blaskic had a command role when the area was ethnically cleansed by Bosnian Croat forces, with hundreds of civilians killed during the razing of Moslem villages.
He is charged with grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions governing conduct during wartime, violations of the laws and customs of war and crimes against humanity.

Blaskic was a career officer in the federal Yugoslav army before the country's break-up, holding the rank of captain. In 1992 he became a colonel in the Bosnian Croat militia and was promoted to general in 1994.
The tribunal has, in total, indicted 75 war crimes suspects -- 54 Serbs (one of whom has since died), 18 Croats and three Moslems -- but has only eight in its custody.
It has no police force of its own and relies on the former Yugoslav republics, other states or the international peace force (SFOR) in Bosnia to make arrests.
The two most prominent indicted suspects are former Bosnian Serb leader Radovan Karadzic and former Bosnian Serb military commander Ratko Mladic, both of whom remain at large.
The Blaskic case will be heard by judges Claude Jorda of France, Fouad Riad of Egypt and Mohamed Shahabuddeen of Guyana.
